{{Short description|Matrix consisting of linearly independent solutions to a linear differential equation}}
{{dablink|For other senses of the term, see [[Fundamental matrix (disambiguation)]].}}

In [[mathematics]], a '''fundamental matrix''' of a system of ''n'' homogeneous linear ordinary differential equations<math display="block"> \dot{\mathbf{x}}(t) = A(t) \mathbf{x}(t) </math>is a matrix-valued function <math> \Psi(t) </math> whose columns are [[linear independence|linearly independent]] solutions of the system.<ref>{{cite book |first=D. |last=Somasundaram |title=Ordinary Differential Equations: A First Course |location=Pangbourne |publisher=Alpha Science |year=2001 |isbn=978-1-84265-069-1 |pages=233–240 |chapter=Fundamental Matrix and Its Properties |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PduY2CjJ1zEC&pg=PA233 }}</ref>
Then every solution to the system can be written as <math>\mathbf{x}(t) = \Psi(t) \mathbf{c}</math>, for some constant vector <math>\mathbf{c}</math> (written as a column vector of height {{mvar|n}}).

A matrix-valued function <math> \Psi </math> is a fundamental matrix of  <math> \dot{\mathbf{x}}(t) = A(t) \mathbf{x}(t) </math> if and only if <math> \dot{\Psi}(t) = A(t) \Psi(t) </math> and <math> \Psi(t) </math> is a [[non-singular matrix]] for all {{nowrap|<math> t </math>.}}<ref>{{cite book |author=Chi-Tsong Chen |year=1998 |title=Linear System Theory and Design |edition=3rd |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=New York |isbn=978-0-19-511777-6 }}</ref> Moreover, if the entries of <math>A(t)</math> are continuous in <math>t</math>, any solution to <math> \dot{\Psi}(t) = A(t) \Psi(t) </math> which is a non-singular matrix for any single value of <math>t</math>, is automatically a non-singular matrix at all other values of <math>t</math>. Thus in this case, to check that <math>\Psi</math> is a fundamental matrix for this equation, it sufficient to check that it is non-singular at a single value of <math>t</math>.

Moreover, if there is at-least one choice of fundamental matrix for a given system, then for each choice of non-singular matrix <math>B</math>, there is exactly one fundamental matrix solution <math>\Psi</math> such that <math>\Psi(0)=B</math><ref>{{cite book |first=D. |last=Somasundaram |title=Ordinary Differential Equations: A First Course |location=Pangbourne |publisher=Alpha Science |year=2001 |isbn=978-1-84265-069-1 |pages=233–240 |chapter=Fundamental Matrix and Its Properties |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PduY2CjJ1zEC&pg=PA233 }}</ref>. The same result holds if <math>0</math> is replaced with any fixed value <math>t_0</math>. Also, if <math>\Psi_0</math> is any fundamental matrix for this equation, then for any non-singular matrix <math>C</math>, the matrix <math>\Psi(t)=\Psi_0(t)C</math> is also a fundamental matrix. In particular, if <math>\Psi_0</math> is any fixed fundamental solution for a given equation, then all other fundamental solutions for this equation are of the form <math>\Psi_0(t)C</math>.

==Control theory==
The fundamental matrix is used to express the [[state-transition matrix]], an essential component in the solution of a system of linear ordinary differential equations.<ref>{{cite book |first=Donald E. |last=Kirk |title=Optimal Control Theory |location=Englewood Cliffs |publisher=Prentice-Hall |year=1970 |pages=19–20 |isbn=978-0-13-638098-6 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=onuH0PnZwV4C&pg=PA19 }}</ref>
